title: "Completed it, mate": teacher identity and Australia's reading wars
author: Haili Hughes
summary: Haili Hughes reflects on encountering Australia's reading wars after moving from England, noting that the same tribal accusations - explicit-teaching advocates cast as cruel, inquiry-learning advocates cast as naive - are repeating a cycle she already lived through in the UK a decade earlier. Her central argument is that the debate's hostility is best explained by identity, not stubbornness: teachers who have built twenty years of professional self-understanding around an approach experience evidence against it as an attack on their competence and training, not a neutral update. She insists this diagnosis does not excuse contempt or evidence-dismissal on either side, and that legitimate questions about research quality and implementation deserve real answers rather than moral point-scoring. Citing England's stable PISA 2025 reading performance against a declining OECD average, she argues the profession should stay curious about what sustained investment in early phonics may have contributed, while resisting both uncritical phonics triumphalism and reflexive dismissal. She closes by arguing Australia's path forward depends less on winning the argument and more on how teachers who followed prior official advice are treated as the evidence shifts under them.
points: Diagnoses the reading-wars hostility as an identity threat rather than a stubbornness problem: teachers who spent decades building professional self-understanding around an approach hear evidence against it as an accusation that their training and expertise were inadequate.

Coins 'nobody gets the T-shirt' to argue that teaching-as-a-learning-profession requires accepting ongoing revision of one's own practice, and applies the same demand for intellectual honesty to explicit-teaching advocates as to inquiry-learning advocates.

Explicitly separates legitimate methodological disagreement (research quality, implementation fidelity) from identity-defense dressed as disagreement, arguing the former deserves real answers while the latter escalates into contempt.

Uses England's PISA 2025 reading stability against OECD-wide decline as a specific, bounded evidence claim - deliberately avoiding the overreach of claiming an international league table proves any single policy caused the result.

Reframes the practical lever for change in Australia as psychological safety, not better evidence: humiliating teachers for following official advice they were given makes them defensive rather than reflective, since universities and employers established the prior practices in the first place.
quotes: If you are a fan of explicit teaching, you are some kind of cruel fascist who hates kids. If you are an inquiry fan, then you are a raging hippy who also hates kids. Both views are silly and oversimplified of course.

If you have spent twenty years believing that the way you teach reading nurtures children's confidence and independence, being told that aspects of that approach are poorly supported by evidence is unlikely to feel like an interesting academic update.
I suspect some of the anger we see in these debates grows from that discomfort. Defending an approach can become a way of defending the teacher you believe yourself to have been.
Nobody gets to buy a T-shirt saying Completed it, mate and retire from thinking about their practice.
That expectation applies equally to those of us who advocate explicit teaching. If we demand intellectual honesty from others, we have to practise it ourselves.
In PISA 2025, its reading performance remained stable while the OECD average declined, leaving only three participating education systems scoring significantly higher.

Humiliating teachers for following advice they were given is unlikely to help them examine it honestly, especially when universities, employers and professional learning providers helped establish those practices in the first place.
Understanding why someone feels defensive gives us a responsibility to support them through change; it does not remove the need for change.
